sources.title: UNESCO: Angkor
sources.note: Direct World Heritage description, Brief synthesis and management discussion. Ninth-to-fifteenth-century capitals, regional influence and inhabited rice-growing villages. The 400 square kilometres is the archaeological park, not the full medieval city or empire.

sources.title: UNESCO: Koh Ker, ancient Lingapura or Chok Gargyar
sources.note: Direct Brief synthesis: established 921, rival capital until 928, sole capital 928 to 944, political centre then returned to Angkor; monolithic stone construction.

sources.title: APSARA National Authority: Angkor Wat
sources.note: Full indexed original read: Suryavarman II, 1113 to 1150 construction/reign, Vishnu dedication, sixteenth-century regional Buddhist pilgrimage. Avoid uncertain exact construction duration and inconsistent area claims.

sources.title: APSARA National Authority: Bayon
sources.note: Full indexed original via exact URL and fish query. Late-twelfth-century Jayavarman VII temple, Buddha under Naga, provincial deities; market stalls, road workers and women preparing fish. Do not adopt contested tower counts or diagnose depicted illness.

sources.title: APSARA National Authority: Elephant Terrace
sources.note: Direct fetch 403; full indexed original returned with site:apsaraauthority.gov.kh/2021/08/13/elephant-terrace/ "daily". 300-metre terrace, wooden pavilions, excavated postholes and attributed late-thirteenth-century Zhou Daguan royal audience account.

sources.title: Alison Carter and colleagues: Prasat and Pteah, habitation within Angkor Wat’s temple enclosure
sources.note: Direct accepted-manuscript PDF. PDF pages 13 to 17, numbered manuscript pages 13 to 17: possible hearths, habitation evidence, lack of complete house plan, rice husks, gardens and cotton. The posthole household study is primary; botanical details cite Castillo et al. 2020 within it. All three resulting passages together stay below 200 words.

sources.title: University of Sydney: Angkor’s water network and climate stress
sources.note: Direct research-team institutional account, 18 October 2018, Science Advances network study. Canal/catchment/embankment systems; modeled vulnerability from prolonged drought followed by wet years. Not treated as sole established cause of decline.

sources.title: Siddham: Say Fong hospital inscription K.368, translations
sources.note: Direct scholarly epigraphy database: Louis Finot 1903 French translation stanzas 19 to 41 provides staff/supplies. Honda English stanza 17 gives 1108 Saka/1186 CE. French and English are editions of the same historical inscription, not independent hospital censuses.

sources.title: DHARMA: Hospital east of Ta Keo, inscription K.537
sources.note: Direct digital edition by Kunthea Chhom, title 1108 Saka. Language Sanskrit, script Khmer. Face A line 1 exactly namo vuddhāya. This is scholarly Roman transliteration; original Khmer letterforms not reconstructed. Translation section is empty; meaning checked against Honda’s separately translated parallel hospital formula.

sources.title: Megumu Honda: The Say-Fong inscription of Jayavarman VII (1965)
sources.note: Direct 13-page scholarly PDF. Printed page 415, PDF page 3, stanza 1 gives namo buddhaya in extracted Roman text and Salutation to Buddha!; opening corresponds to K.537 vuddhāya spelling. Printed page 408, PDF page 10, stanza 17 converts 1108 Saka to 1186 CE. PDF screenshot failed; extracted text directly read. Our short English gloss is a paraphrase, not presented as Honda’s exact wording.

sources.title: Queen Indradevi: From the Great Stele of Phimeanakas, translated by Trent Walker
sources.note: Direct translated primary poem and editorial introduction, 2 November 2015. Composition circa 1190 to 1200, 102 stanzas, sister Jayarajadevi and husband Jayavarman VII. Learning passage paraphrased; no quotation or claim of universal schooling.

sources.title: University of Sydney: New research on Angkor’s gradual decline
sources.note: Direct research-team account, 26 February 2019, Penny and colleagues PNAS sediment study. Angkor Thom moat cores, early-fourteenth-century falling erosion/burning/disturbance, late-fourteenth-century floating vegetation. Evidence specific to administrative centre; no universal abandonment in 1431.

proposedOverrides.name: Khmer Empire
proposedOverrides.summary: Angkorian Khmer power joined monumental temples, water engineering and inhabited landscapes across mainland Southeast Asia.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One existing indexed entity, no aliases or new geometry.
batchIdentityNotes.actualSnapshots: Seven decoded mainland Southeast Asian snapshots from 900 to 1492; precise intervals and bounding boxes in ../identity-all-snapshots.json.
batchIdentityNotes.publicCaveat: Opening distinguishes map coverage from founding/fall and broad outline from exact imperial control. Khmer people and Angkor religious life continue after political transformation.
batchIdentityNotes.navigation: No successor links proposed; regional conflict is discussed without assigning a single fall year or unverified target geometry.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: K.537 hospital east of Ta Keo, Sanskrit in Khmer script, 1108 Saka/1186 CE. Exact scholarly Roman transliteration preserved; short English gloss checked against parallel translated K.368 invocation.
